Please review the following manuscript. I feel disappointed with this paper. My overall impression is poor, and I'd be concerned to see it accepted.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b09/review-experiment-wihn3g05/call-59524403e8de44ba8b6614dce09c870a/manuscript.pdf

strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment problem. Combining density-ratio estimation with weighted score calibration is a sensible approach under covariate shift and support overlap, without modifying the monitored classifier.

The evaluation is substantial within the census domain: 959 model–dataset cases and 36,557 production chunks. PAPE improves all six aggregate results in Table 1; comparisons with importance weighting and unweighted CBPE provide useful evidence for the proposed combination.

The high-level algorithm is understandable. Public datasets, a code link, and explicit discussion of concept shift, missing support, calibration error, and sampling uncertainty are positive aspects of research transparency.
weaknesses: The central estimator does not support the claimed metric generality as written. Equations (1)–(2) cover expectations of per-example quantities, whereas F1 is a ratio of aggregate counts and AUROC is a pairwise ranking statistic. Both require additional estimators and analysis that are absent, despite constituting two of the three evaluated metrics. This leaves a material gap between the specified algorithm, theoretical claims, and experiments.

The theoretical guarantee largely assumes the difficult part: accurate target calibration obtained using appropriate importance weights. It does not characterize errors from the learned density ratios and calibrator. Equation (4) also incorrectly equates expected absolute label residual with absolute conditional calibration error; the former remains positive even for a perfectly calibrated, nondeterministic label distribution. The intended additive-metric argument is recoverable, but the theory needs correction and clearer scope.

Important implementation details are missing from the manuscript, including the density-ratio classifier, calibrator family and objective, preprocessing, and relevant hyperparameters. Algorithm 1 evaluates the density-ratio classifier on its training reference inputs without specifying safeguards against overfitting. The code link is helpful, but the paper does not sufficiently specify the components driving its results.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently reported. The paired Wilcoxon result is given as p = 0.0 without identifying the pairing unit or addressing dependencies among chunks and models sharing data. Chunk-level aggregation also gives larger datasets more influence. Per-task/state results and uncertainty estimates accounting for shared data are needed to establish how broadly the improvements hold.

Experimental breadth is narrower than the headline case count suggests: all tasks use the same census source. Temporal changes are not established to satisfy covariate shift, and no controlled experiments isolate the effects of shift severity, support overlap, or density-ratio accuracy. The sample-size study covers only one selected case, limiting conclusions about robustness.

Originality and scope are overstated relative to the evidence. The method combines established importance weighting, calibration, and conditional expectation, but its distinction from prior weighted-calibration work is not developed sufficiently. Moreover, the abstract's claim of relying only on predictions and probabilities conflicts with Algorithm 1's requirement for feature inputs. These issues, together with the incomplete metric specification and experimental reporting, outweigh the promising empirical results.
